pair01.why: Near identical. A's 'Unrelated to the above, I renamed' is a stock aside; B's 'With it off, nothing changes for users' and 'if you have a minute' read slightly more natural. Both cover every fact.

pair02.why: A's bold 'Testing' and 'Other changes' headers over one-line bullets plus the robot footer look templated. B has a title and prose but buries '140 lines' in its own paragraph. Both carry the footer and all facts.

pair03.why: B opens with the support action ('tell them to try the payment again... not charged'). A's opening sentences restate the incident and put the action in a later 'What to tell affected customers' line. A's 'not actually declined' is slightly more formulaic.

A: I have not committed to anything
B: I haven't replied, since B is out
I'll convert the Vendor C trial before it ends

pair04.why: Both open with the recommendation and deadline. B's tidy 'Vendor B is the cheapest, but it fails Legal's requirement. Vendor A fails Security's.' arithmetic is polished, but it adds a reply status and a conversion step the task never gave. A invents less.

pair05.why: B states 'The two cheaper options each miss one requirement' before the bullets, so the reason they are out is clear at once. A adds the price differences and a closing 'Can you approve the spend before the 28th?', which makes it a bit more templated.

A: nothing on the export is waiting on design input

pair06.why: B is a tight chat reply: 'Probably, but it depends on one bug fix landing on time' plus the UTC bug and the 3pm freeze. A pads with the designer on leave, which is irrelevant to the question, and adds the claim 'nothing on the export is waiting on design input'.

A: I'll move us to Vendor C's paid plan before the trial ends

pair07.why: B leads with the request and 'The two cheaper options each fail a requirement', then closes on the ask. A adds an annual cost figure and 'recommendation is based on running all three, not only on their websites', which is typical model self-justification, plus a plan to move to the paid plan.

A: I'd move the release to next week
B: I'll tell you by Thursday afternoon
I'll deploy Thursday or first thing Friday

pair08.why: B uses 'Short answer:', 'Where it stands:' and 'The risks I see:' headers with bullets in a chat reply, and promises specific timings the task never gave. A is shorter and starts 'Maybe. It ships Friday only if...'. A still invents a fallback plan.

pair09.why: A's first two sentences say 'The incident is resolved. Card payments at checkout are working again.' B opens with the outage window and error, and only reaches 'resolved' in sentence four. A's 'What support should do' and 'What engineering is doing' headers are more templated, and 'the problem was on our side' is a small inference.

B: most of them the polling code

pair10.why: B claims the 140 removed lines are 'most of them the polling code', which the task did not say. A puts the SSE change and the flag in its first two sentences and asks for a specific Firefox check, without inventing.

B: we have Friday morning to verify it
I'd hold the export rather than ship wrong dates

pair11.why: A answers 'Yes, if the last bug fix lands on Thursday' and says the fix 'has to be merged and deployed' before the 3pm freeze, which is exactly the dependency the PM needs. B adds a Friday-morning verification step and a hold decision that the task did not give.

A: The certificate should have renewed automatically

pair12.why: A's second sentence is the support action: 'tell them to try the payment again. They were not charged.' B has the same facts but spreads them across bold labels such as 'What to tell affected customers:', which feels like a template. B's 'It should go through' is a small unsupported assurance.
